title: Two hydrogen-burning engines powered this car to a new land speed record
gist: JCB's Hydromax, powered by two heavily modified versions of the company's own hydrogen combustion engine making 800 hp each, set a 406.320 mph two-way average at Bonneville — more than double the 2004 BMW H2R hydrogen record and well clear of both the fuel-cell (303 mph) and battery-electric (341 mph) marks.

insights.claim: JCB built prototype hydrogen fuel cell machines and abandoned the technology as too expensive and too fragile for farm and construction site duty, pivoting in 2020 to developing its own hydrogen combustion engine instead.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A major equipment OEM concluding fuel cells fail on cost and durability in dirty, high-vibration environments is a real-world verdict against fuel cells in off-highway machinery.
insights.quote: At first, that meant fuel cells, but after developing prototypes, JCB concluded the tech was too expensive and too fragile for life on the farm or the construction site.

insights.claim: JCB's hydrogen engine deliberately reuses diesel engine architecture — same family design, turbocharged, running at very low revs — with hydrogen injected at much lower pressure and temperature than diesel and ignited by spark.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Reusing diesel architecture preserves existing manufacturing lines and supply chains — the strongest economic argument for hydrogen ICE over any clean-sheet zero-emission powertrain.
insights.quote: JCB decided to build an entirely new hydrogen engine, drawing on its experience developing diesel engines and sharing much of the engine architecture.
insights.locator: A cutaway of the JCB Hydromax

insights.claim: JCB's motivation is regulatory: as a UK-based manufacturer it cannot ignore carbon emissions targets and must have alternatives to diesel, splitting its response between batteries for some products and hydrogen for others.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Emissions regulation is the forcing function pushing heavy-equipment OEMs into dual-track powertrain R&D — a durable cost and capex burden for the sector.
insights.quote: And as JCB is based in the UK, it doesn’t have the luxury of being able to ignore carbon emissions targets; it has to have alternatives to diesel engines.
insights.locator: JCB is a UK-based manufacturer of heavy industrial

insights.claim: Prior hydrogen ICE attempts were poor: BMW's 2006 hydrogen-converted naturally aspirated V12 in a 7 Series ran at 60 percent of gasoline power with five times the fuel consumption, while Toyota's endurance-racing Corolla used a turbocharged three-cylinder to partly offset hydrogen's lower energy density.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: The historical 60 percent power and 5x consumption penalty quantifies exactly what forced induction and direct injection had to overcome — the benchmark for judging progress in hydrogen ICE.
insights.quote: in 2006, BMW modified a naturally aspirated V12 engine in a 7 Series to run on hydrogen, which it did, but with 60 percent of the power and five times the fuel consumption compared to gasoline
insights.locator: The idea of burning hydrogen in an internal combustion engine

insights.claim: JCB took a production hydrogen engine making 74 hp (55 kW) and extracted 800 hp (597 kW) from each of the two units in the Hydromax — roughly an eleven-fold increase in output from the same base architecture.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: An 11x output scaling demonstrates hydrogen combustion has substantial headroom, undercutting the assumption that hydrogen ICE is inherently power-limited.
insights.quote: each of the two hydrogen engines powering the JCB Hydromax has been seriously worked on, increasing their outputs to 800 hp (597 kW) apiece
insights.locator: Performance might match JCB’s diesel engines

insights.claim: Achieving that output required doubling engine speed to 3,800 rpm, replacing pushrod valves with double overhead camshafts for timing control, moving to direct injection at far higher pressure, dry-sumping, weight reduction and improved cooling.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: The modification list shows the production engine's limits were valvetrain and fueling, not combustion chemistry — a roadmap for where hydrogen ICE component suppliers matter.
insights.quote: That required doubling the engine speed to a heady 3,800 rpm, replacing the pushrod valves with double overhead camshafts for better control over timing, and moving to direct fuel injection at much higher pressure than the production engine.
insights.locator: Performance might match JCB’s diesel engines

insights.claim: The Hydromax uses two ice tanks to chill post-turbocharger air from 392°F (200°C) to below 50°F (10°C), an extreme charge-cooling solution that is race-specific and not transferable to production machinery.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Ice-tank intercooling is the tell that this output level is not thermally sustainable in a real product — a caution against reading the record as a commercial capability claim.
insights.quote: The JCB Hydromax even uses two ice tanks to cool the air leaving the turbocharger, down from 392° F (200° C) to below 50° F (10° C).

insights.claim: The final car combined 1,600 hp (1,193 kW) and 2,600 lb-ft (3,525 Nm) through all-wheel drive to run 400.623 mph one way and 412.135 mph in the other for a 406.320 mph (653.91 km/h) two-way average.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: The 11.5 mph spread between runs indicates conditions or setup variance, which is the practical margin remaining if JCB returns for a higher number.
insights.quote: the JCB Hydromax set a speed of 400.623 mph (644.74 km/h) yesterday, followed by a run in the other direction of 412.135 mph (663.27 km/h) for a two-way average of 406.320 mph (653.91 km/h)

themes.theme: Where the record sits in the hierarchy

insights.claim: The Hydromax's 406.320 mph is more than double the previous hydrogen combustion record of 185.5 mph set by the BMW H2R in 2004 using the power-limited hydrogen V12.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A 22-year-old record more than doubled in one attempt indicates the category was dormant rather than saturated — cheap headlines available to any OEM that shows up.
insights.quote: That’s more than twice as fast as the previous hydrogen combustion land speed record of 185.5 mph (298.53 km/h) set by the BMW H2R in 2004

insights.claim: Hydrogen combustion now beats both rival zero-carbon propulsion records: the fuel-cell mark of 303 mph set by the Venturi Buckeye Bullet 2 in 2009 and the battery-electric mark of 341 mph set by VBB3 in 2016.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Hydrogen ICE leapfrogging both fuel cells and batteries on peak output is a marketing asset for hydrogen advocates arguing combustion deserves a second look.
insights.quote: it’s a lot faster than the fastest hydrogen fuel cell speed record as well, which stands at 303 mph (488 km/h), set by the Venturi Buckeye Bullet 2 in 2009. It also beats the fastest EV land speed record, which was set in 2016 by VBB3 at 341 mph (549 km/h).
insights.locator: That’s more than twice as fast as the previous hydrogen

insights.claim: The Hydromax remains well short of the nitromethane-fueled Challenger II's 449 mph wheel-driven record from 2018 and far below Thrust SSC's 763.6 mph absolute mark from 1997, which still stands because Bloodhound's 1,000 mph attempt ran out of money.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Context matters for how the record should be valued — this is a category record, not an absolute one, and the absolute mark has gone unchallenged for nearly 30 years on funding grounds.
insights.quote: Thrust SSC’s two-way average of 763.6 mph (1,229 km/h), set in 1997, remains the fastest anyone has ever driven a wheeled vehicle over a timed mile.
insights.locator: It’s been far too long since I’ve been able to report

insights.claim: The driver was RAF Wing Commander Andy Green, who broke the sound barrier in Thrust SSC in 1997 and set JCB's diesel land speed record of 350 mph with the Dieselmax in 2006 — the same driver-manufacturer pairing twenty years apart.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: JCB's repeat use of record attempts as a technology showcase, two decades apart, signals this is a deliberate brand strategy rather than a one-off stunt.
insights.quote: He also drove Thrust SSC through the sound barrier in 1997, and in 2006, he set a diesel-powered land speed record, again with JCB, with the JCB Dieselmax, which topped out at 350 mph (563 km/h).
insights.locator: Behind the wheel yesterday was RAF Wing Commander Andy Green
